topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: How are positions along a large aircraft's structure usually identified?

options.text: By the seat row numbers only
By measuring from the CG every time a part is located
By stations, water lines and buttock lines

explanation: Large aircraft are divided about their three axes by station numbers, water lines and buttock lines, rather than by measuring from the datum each time.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: On a stretched variant of an aircraft, why may station numbers no longer equal balance arms?

options.text: The datum is moved to the CG on every variant
Station numbers are always measured from the tail
Fuselage sections were inserted but the old numbers kept
The MAC becomes longer on a stretched variant

explanation: New variants are often made by inserting fuselage plugs. Keeping the original station numbers means some stations no longer match their distance from the datum, so a conversion chart is needed.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: A stretched variant has a fuselage plug inserted ahead of the wing. What is needed to find the balance arm of a station in the forward fuselage?

options.text: Nothing at all; the station number is always the arm

explanation: Where stations and arms no longer coincide, the manufacturer's conversion chart turns a station number into a balance arm and back.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: A 100 in plug is inserted ahead of the wing, and the datum is at the nose. A forward-fuselage item aft of the plug has the same structural station number as before. How has its balance arm changed?
explanation: Everything behind the plug is now 100 in further from the nose datum, so its balance arm increases by 100 in even though the station number is the same.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: Why can moving the flaps on a large aircraft change the CG?

options.text: The flap and slat mass moves fore and aft
The datum moves with the flaps
Flaps change the length of the MAC
Flap movement changes the aircraft's total mass

explanation: Extending or retracting flaps moves their mass along the fuselage axis, so the total moment changes. The manual gives the moment change for each flap movement.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: Trailing edge flaps that move aft and down are extended. What happens to the total moment?

options.text: It decreases, moving the CG forward
It increases, moving the CG forward
It increases, moving the CG aft

explanation: Extending flaps that travel aft increases the moment about the datum, so the CG moves slightly aft; retracting them has the opposite effect.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: An aeroplane of 60 000 kg has its CG at 640 in. Retracting the flaps causes a moment change of −15 000 kg in. What is the new CG?
explanation: Δcg = −15 000 ÷ 60 000 = −0.25 in, so the CG moves forward to 639.75 in.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: Why is the stabiliser trim set for take-off according to the CG?

options.text: To reduce the stalling speed on the runway
To give the elevator enough authority to rotate and control the aircraft
To trim out the yaw of an engine failure on take-off
To prevent the nose wheel from shimmying

explanation: The take-off stabiliser setting lets the elevator rotate the aeroplane on the take-off run and control it in the first stage of flight. The CG position decides the setting.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: How does the take-off stabiliser trim setting change as the CG moves forward?
explanation: A more forward CG gives a stronger nose-down moment, so more nose-up stabiliser trim units are needed for rotation.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: How does a larger take-off flap setting usually affect the required nose-up stabiliser trim for the same CG?

options.text: No change, because flap does not affect trim

explanation: Typical trim charts show a slightly smaller nose-up setting at the higher flap setting for the same % MAC.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: Why must the commander know the underload?

options.text: To know what extra load can be accepted
To know how much fuel can be jettisoned in flight

explanation: The underload is the spare traffic load capacity. It tells the commander whether last minute additions (extra passengers or cargo) can be accepted.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: Why is the underload not simply the regulated take-off mass minus the actual take-off mass?

options.text: The underload is always zero for large aircraft
The regulated take-off mass already includes the traffic load
The taxi fuel must be added to it
ZFM and landing limits also apply

explanation: Extra traffic load also raises the zero fuel mass and the landing mass. If the aeroplane is already at its MZFM there is no underload at all, whatever the take-off margin.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: An aeroplane is already loaded to its maximum zero fuel mass. What is its underload?

options.text: The difference between RTOM and actual TOM

explanation: Any extra traffic load would exceed the MZFM, so the underload is zero.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: How is the structurally limited traffic load found?
explanation: The structural limit on the traffic load is the maximum zero fuel mass minus the dry operating mass.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: How is the take-off limited traffic load found?
explanation: Take-off limited traffic load = regulated take-off mass − DOM − take-off fuel.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: How is the landing limited traffic load found?
explanation: Landing limited traffic load = regulated landing mass − DOM − fuel remaining at landing (contingency, alternate and reserve).

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: Which value is the allowed traffic load?

options.text: The highest of the three limited values
The lowest of the three limited values
The average of the three limited values, rounded down

explanation: All three limits must be respected, so the allowed traffic load is the lowest of the three.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: MZFM 52 000 kg, RTOM 64 000 kg, RLM 55 000 kg, DOM 35 000 kg, take-off fuel 13 000 kg, fuel at landing 4 500 kg. What is the allowed traffic load?
explanation: Structural 52 000 − 35 000 = 17 000; take-off 64 000 − 35 000 − 13 000 = 16 000; landing 55 000 − 35 000 − 4 500 = 15 500. The lowest, 15 500 kg, is landing limited.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: With an allowed traffic load of 15 500 kg and an actual traffic load of 14 800 kg, what is the underload?
explanation: Underload = allowed traffic load − actual traffic load = 15 500 − 14 800 = 700 kg.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: On the load and trim sheet, the allowable take-off mass is the lowest of which three values?

options.text: MZFM + take-off fuel; RTOM; RLM + trip fuel
MZFM + trip fuel; RTOM; RLM + take-off fuel

explanation: The three possible take-off masses are: loaded to MZFM plus the take-off fuel; the regulated take-off mass; and landing at the regulated landing mass plus the trip fuel added back.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: MZFM 52 000 kg, take-off fuel 13 000 kg, RTOM 64 000 kg, RLM 55 000 kg and trip fuel 8 500 kg. What is the allowable take-off mass?
explanation: MZFM + TOF = 65 000; RTOM = 64 000; RLM + trip = 63 500. The lowest is 63 500 kg, so landing is the limit.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: On the load and trim sheet, how is the maximum allowable traffic load found from the allowable take-off mass?

options.text: Allowable take-off mass minus operating mass
Allowable take-off mass minus take-off fuel

explanation: Operating mass (DOM + take-off fuel) is everything except the traffic load, so allowable TOM − OM = maximum traffic load.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: The allowable take-off mass is 63 500 kg, the DOM 35 000 kg and the take-off fuel 13 000 kg. What is the maximum traffic load?
explanation: OM = 35 000 + 13 000 = 48 000 kg; maximum traffic load = 63 500 − 48 000 = 15 500 kg, matching the three-formula method.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: Regulated take-off mass 63 000 kg, DOM 35 200 kg (crew included), take-off fuel 15 200 kg. Landing and zero fuel limits are not limiting. Passengers and their baggage total 11 638 kg. What is the most freight that can be loaded?
explanation: Allowed traffic = 63 000 − 35 200 − 15 200 = 12 600 kg; freight = 12 600 − 11 638 = 962 kg. Forgetting to subtract the passengers gives 12 600 kg.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: What does the underload set a limit on?

options.text: Last minute changes to the load
The amount of extra fuel that can be jettisoned
The trip fuel for the flight

explanation: The underload sets the limiting mass for last minute changes (LMC) to the traffic load.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: An aeroplane has a large underload, and the commander decides to take extra fuel. What happens to the underload?

options.text: It increases by the mass of the fuel
It may be used up by the extra fuel

explanation: Extra fuel uplift raises the take-off and landing masses, so it can consume some or all of the underload.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: Which side of a combined load and trim sheet is the loading summary?

options.text: There is no loading summary on it

explanation: Part A on the left itemises the masses and their distribution (DOM, traffic load and fuel). Part B on the right shows how each mass affects the CG relative to the MAC.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: In part A of the load sheet, what is section 1 used for?

options.text: Limiting TOM, traffic load and underload
The distribution of the passengers by cabin zone and seat row

explanation: Section 1 sets the limiting take-off mass, the maximum allowable traffic load and the underload before last minute changes. Section 2 distributes the traffic load and section 3 summarises and cross-checks.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: On a load sheet, what does the abbreviation "TR" mean?
explanation: In the traffic load distribution section, TR is transit, B baggage, C cargo, M mail and Pax passengers (F first, C club/business, Y economy).

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: On a load sheet, what does "M" stand for in the traffic load distribution?
explanation: The abbreviations are TR transit, B baggage, C cargo, M mail and Pax passengers.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: On a load sheet, what does "Pax Y" refer to?
explanation: Pax F is first class, Pax C club/business and Pax Y economy.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: In part B (trim) of the load and trim sheet, what is the starting value?
explanation: The dry operating index for the DOM is entered at the top, then moved through each row of boxes for the cargo and passenger zones.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: In part B, how is each row of boxes used?

options.text: Each row adds a fixed index of 1
The rows are only used for fuel
The index is multiplied by the number shown in the row
The index moves by the row's pitch

explanation: Each box has a pitch representing a mass or a number of persons and an arrow for the direction; the line moves along the row by the load in that zone.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: After the last traffic load row in part B, what is checked?

options.text: That the take-off fuel index is positive
That the landing mass is below the maximum structural landing mass
That the ZFM point is in its envelope

explanation: A line is dropped from the index at the last row to the ZFM on the vertical scale; the point must lie within the zero fuel mass envelope.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: In part B, what is done after the zero fuel mass point is found?

options.text: The fuel index is added and a line dropped to the take-off mass
The trip fuel is subtracted and a line dropped to the landing mass

explanation: The take-off fuel index is applied and a line dropped to the take-off mass on the envelope. That point must lie within the take-off mass envelope.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: If both the zero fuel mass and take-off mass points lie within the envelope, what can be concluded?

options.text: The aeroplane is safe for take-off only
It is safe for the flight and diversions
The trim setting can be ignored
The landing CG must still be calculated separately on the sheet

explanation: With ZFM and TOM within the envelope, the CG remains within limits throughout the flight, including any permitted diversions.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: On a typical twin jet, which fuel is normally used first?
explanation: Centre tank fuel is normally used before wing tank fuel. Keeping fuel in the wings for longer relieves wing root bending.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: The DOM CG is at 18% of a 134 in MAC whose leading edge is 625 in aft of the datum. What is the DOM balance arm?
explanation: 0.18 × 134 = 24.1 in; 625 + 24.1 ≈ 649 in aft of the datum. This arm, times the DOM, gives the DOM moment for the manifest.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: Why is a load sheet individual to each aircraft type?

options.text: Each type has its own standard passenger masses

explanation: Load sheets reflect the type's own structure: its mass limits, compartment arms and CG envelope. It must be compiled before each flight.

topic: 10 Large Aircraft Loading and Load Sheets
question: In the traffic load calculation, unused contingency fuel is treated as part of which figure?
explanation: Fuel remaining at landing includes the contingency, alternate and reserve fuel when no eventualities occur, which is why it appears in the landing limited traffic load.
